Vision--language--action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for robot learning, integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation across diverse manipulation tasks and robot embodiments~\cite{rt2,openvla,pi0,wang2026limitsvisionandlanguagenavigation,wang2025dreamnavtrajectorybasedimaginativeframework}.
By learning instruction-conditioned behaviors from demonstrations, these models provide a unified framework for translating multimodal inputs into robot actions.
Extending VLA learning to humanoid robots could enable a broader range of tasks in human environments, where locomotion, posture adjustment, and object manipulation must be coordinated~\cite{grootn1,psi0,openhlm}.
For example, transferring an object between tables requires coordinated grasping, turning, walking, and placement while maintaining balance (Fig.~\ref{fig:overview}, bottom).
Such tasks require policies that translate task intent and visual feedback into coherent whole-body action sequences.
Humanoid VLA learning thus offers a path toward connecting multimodal task understanding with coordinated whole-body behavior, motivating the extension of existing robot policy architectures to loco-manipulation.

A common approach to humanoid policy learning extends the backbone--action expert paradigm established in robotic manipulation to whole-body control.
In this paradigm, pretrained vision--language models provide semantic representations of instructions and observations (Fig.~\ref{fig:policy_routes}(a))~\cite{grootn1,psi0,openhlm}, while video generation models contribute spatiotemporal priors for scene evolution (Fig.~\ref{fig:policy_routes}(b))~\cite{motionwam,wholebodywam_wbc}.
These representations condition action generation, producing motion references or control commands.
Adapting this paradigm to humanoids requires organizing control over root motion, body articulation, and hand interaction.
Representative designs either generate whole-body action sequences within a shared predictor (Fig.~\ref{fig:policy_routes}(d))~\cite{openhlm,motionwam}, or produce upper-body joint targets together with lower-body locomotion commands executed by a dedicated controller (Fig.~\ref{fig:policy_routes}(e))~\cite{humanoidexo,wholebodyvla}.
Unified generation captures cross-component dependencies within a shared predictor, while the hybrid design combines direct upper-body control with learned locomotion and stabilization.
Both provide practical routes for transferring pretrained semantic and visual dynamics knowledge to humanoid loco-manipulation.
